topics.title: This is a fun problem
topics.text:
There are four men who want to cross a bridge. They all begin on the same side. You have 17 minutes to get all of them across to the other side. It is night. There is one flashlight. A maximum of two people can cross at one time. Any party who crosses, either one or two people, must have the flashlight with them. The flashlight must be walked back and forth, it cannot be thrown, etc. Each man walks at a different speed. A pair must walk together at the rate of the slower man

Man 1: 1 minute to cross

Man 2: 2 minutes to cross

Man 3: 5 minutes to cross

Man 4: 10 minutes to cross

For example, if Man 1 and Man 4 walk across first, 10 minutes have elapsed when they get to the other side of the bridge. If Man 4 returns with the flashlight, a total of 20 minutes have passed, and you have failed the mission.

topics.title: Competition Math for Middle School by J. Batterson..mistake?
topics.text:
I finished this book earlier, but I didn't look at the solutions to find faster solutions. I did it again recently, looking at all of the solutions, and there was one solution that I disagreed with. The problem and solution are as follows:



Problem: How many whole numbers less than 100 are multiples of 3 but not multiples of 5?



Solution: There are 33 multiples of 3 [whole numbers less than 100] (3 x 1 through 3 x 33). Multiples of 3 that are multiples of 5 are multiples of 15. Six multiples of 15 (15 x 1 through 15 x 6) must be excluded to give us 27 whole numbers.



I agree with the answer, but not the solution. From what I know, 0 is a multiple of all numbers for anything times zero is equal to zero. In the first part, shouldn't it say "There are 34 multiples of 3", for zero is a whole number and multiple of 3, and same for the third sentence? The reason I'm posting this is because I think there is some kind of reason why the author didn't write the phrase "natural numbers" instead of "whole numbers". Writing this would make more sense. Or, the author could have also put 34 multiples instead of 33. Any thoughts?

topics.title: 9 A well-known problem in math and philosophy
topics.text:
A very intelligent host offers you two boxes on a game show, Box 1 and Box 2. Box 1 is clear and contains $1000, and Box 2 is opaque and contains either $0 or $1,000,000 (depending on the choice of the host). The host offers you the choice to either take both boxes, or take only box 2.



Before the show, the host makes a prediction on whether you will choose both boxes or only Box 2. If the host predicted that you take both boxes, he put $0 in Box 2. If the host predicted that you only take Box 2, then he put $1,000,000 in Box 2.



Which box(es) do you take and why?



(In case you're interested, this is Newcomb's problem.)

another way of expressing this could be as a cake with a countably infinite number of layers. the first layer is blue, and then the second one is red. the third, blue, and the fourth, red. you get the idea.

would the last layer be red or blue?
